title: How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
lead: A program is a testable model of a problem, not merely a collection of commands. Start with inputs, rules and observable results.
why: In practice, a developer must reason about requirements, invalid data and test evidence. Compilable code can still compute the wrong answer.
objectives: Distinguish the problem statement, algorithm, implementation and tests.
Specify inputs, outputs and boundary cases.
Explain why a successful build does not establish correctness.
Change a program and demonstrate the effect with reproducible tests.
prerequisites: Variables, conditions and compilers are introduced from first principles.

concepts.definition: Data supplied for a particular execution of a program.
A constraint under which the requested behavior is defined.
A concrete input together with the expected observable result.
A tool that checks and translates C++ source for the build process.

sections.title: Agree on behavior before writing code
paragraphs: To compute the total for a shopping basket, we need a unit price, quantity and a rule: price multiplied by quantity. The requirement is incomplete until invalid inputs and numeric bounds have been discussed.
A table of cases makes expectations explicit: 120 and 3 must yield 360; 120 and 0 must yield 0; a negative price must be rejected or handled under an agreed policy.

sections.title: An algorithm bridges a requirement and a programming language
paragraphs: An algorithm specifies the necessary steps: read values, check them, compute a result and produce output. It can be expressed without using C++ syntax at all.
The same steps can be implemented in different languages. The required outcome remains the benchmark against which each implementation is evaluated.

sections.title: What happens when C++ is executed
paragraphs: A developer edits source files; compilation checks the language rules and translates source; linking assembles required components; execution runs the program. A failure can occur at different stages.

A program using addition instead of multiplication might compile and run without any warning. It is still wrong for this requirement. Debugging means reproducing the mismatch, locating its cause and retesting.

sections.title: Tests are evidence, not decoration
paragraphs: A test case states input, expected output and observed output. Running the same case after a change is regression testing: it checks that a fix did not break behavior that used to work.
Use ordinary, boundary and invalid inputs. A single successful run says very little about the full input space or the quality of a program.

sections.title: A disciplined development cycle
paragraphs: Clarify the problem, model the data, design an algorithm, implement it, run checks, explain results and refine. This ordering reduces random code changes.
Document the accepted inputs, error policy and outputs in words another person can understand. These notes are part of an engineering deliverable.

sections.title: Reading your first C++ program
paragraphs: #include <iostream> makes stream declarations available. int main() is the entry point; braces enclose its body. int price = 120 creates an integer variable with an initial value. The = operator assigns a value; it does not test equality. A simple statement ends with a semicolon.

std::cin >> price >> count reads two whitespace-separated integers. std::cout << total prints the result; \n ends the line. If the stream cannot read a number, !(std::cin >> ...) is true and the program prints invalid. The || operator means logical OR: one failed boundary condition is enough to reject the input.

sections.title: Input policy and execution limits
paragraphs: Price and quantity are integers 0..1000; discount is 0..100. Round the saving down to whole units: total = subtotal − (subtotal·discount)/100. The bounds keep intermediate products within a 32-bit int.

Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

experiments.verification: Run the program and explain how the formula determines the result.

experiments.title: Introduce a logic defect
experiments.prediction: The code still executes but returns 123 instead of 360.
experiments.verification: Use the original test to locate and repair the discrepancy.

diagnostics.symptom: The program builds but prints 123 instead of 360
diagnostics.cause: The arithmetic operator no longer matches the requirement.
diagnostics.fix: Review the original formula and rerun the regression case.

diagnostics.symptom: A negative unit price produces a negative charge
diagnostics.cause: The input policy was not specified or enforced.
diagnostics.fix: Reject invalid input before computing the total.

assessment.question: Why does a successful compilation not prove correctness?
answers: A logic defect may be valid C++
The compiler already knows user requirements
assessment.explanation: Compilation cannot validate your domain requirement.

assessment.question: Which example is a reproducible test?
assessment.explanation: A test requires concrete input and expected output.

assessment.question: What should precede a focused defect fix?
answers: Reproduce the wrong result on a known case
assessment.explanation: A reproducible failure is the starting point for diagnosis.
